opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing I'd do is recognize that those two goals pull in somewhat different directions. Language alignment rewards invariance. You want a photo of a dog, in almost any pose or lighting, to land near the concept "dog," and that's what CLIP-style contrastive training is good at. But fine-grained discrimination needs the details that this invariance tends to throw away: small text in an image, the exact count of objects, the spatial relationship between two things, or the subtle difference between two similar species. So if you train one global embedding and ask it to do both, you usually get a compromise.

So I wouldn't force everything through a single vector. I'd keep a hierarchy of features. The backbone could be a ConvNeXt-like or ViT-like architecture, and honestly, from our work comparing ConvNets and transformers, I don't think the block type is the deciding factor. Training recipe, data, and scale often matter as much or more. What matters more here is preserving high-resolution, spatially rich features at the earlier and middle stages, while the later stages and a pooled output provide the more semantic representation that aligns well with language.

Then I'd let the language model decide what it needs, rather than compressing the image up front. Instead of handing it a small, fixed set of tokens, you could provide a coarse overview of the whole image plus the ability to query high-resolution regions through cross-attention, or to crop and zoom adaptively. A person looks at a scene and then moves their fovea to the part that matters, and a model could work similarly. If the question is about reading a label in the corner, the text should be able to pull up those high-resolution features. This also helps with cost, because processing everything at full resolution all the time gets expensive quickly, especially for video.

For training, I'd combine objectives. A contrastive or caption-based loss provides language alignment. A self-supervised objective, something in the masked-autoencoder or DINO family, encourages the encoder to retain visual information that captions never mention, because captions are a very lossy description of an image. Most captions won't tell you the texture of a surface or the position of every object. Then, ideally, you fine-tune end to end with the language model on real tasks, such as OCR, counting, and spatial reasoning, because those tasks tell you which details need to survive. And I'd be careful with the data: if you want fine-grained capability, you need hard examples and hard negatives, like near-identical images with different answers, or the model will never be pressured to learn those distinctions.

Finally, I'd evaluate the two goals separately instead of relying on one aggregate benchmark. A model can look great on general VQA while still failing at counting or reading small text, so you want targeted tests that show exactly what information the encoder preserved and what it lost.

r001.rationale: The response proposes combining contrastive or caption-based training for language alignment with self-supervised training to preserve fine-grained visual information.

r002.rationale: It mentions video only in the context of processing cost; it does not propose temporal modeling or world models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly it's one that I think the field has been dancing around for a while without fully resolving. Let me try to unpack it.

So the first thing to say is that these two goals are genuinely in tension, at least with how we train encoders today. If you look at what most multimodal LLMs use, it's some variant of CLIP or SigLIP. And those are great for language alignment, because that's literally what the contrastive objective is optimizing. You're pulling image embeddings toward caption embeddings. But captions are low-bandwidth. A caption says "a dog on a couch." It doesn't say which breed, it doesn't say where the dog's paw is relative to the cushion, it doesn't encode the texture of the fabric. So the encoder learns to throw that information away, because the training signal never rewards keeping it. And then you bolt this thing onto an LLM and ask it to count objects or read small text or tell two similar birds apart, and it struggles, and people act surprised. But it's not surprising. The encoder was told that information was noise.

On the other side, you have encoders trained with self-supervised objectives, DINO, DINOv2, or even just supervised ImageNet classification. Those preserve a lot more fine-grained spatial and textural structure. The features are much more "local" in a sense. But the embedding space has no relationship to language whatsoever. So the projector, that little MLP or whatever you put between the encoder and the LLM, has to do a lot of heavy lifting, and in practice it often can't close that gap with the amount of instruction tuning data people have.

So how would I actually design it? I think there are a few principles.

First, I'd stop thinking of it as one encoder with one objective. The simplest practical thing, and people have done this, is to combine multiple encoders. Take a CLIP-style model and a DINO-style model, concatenate or interleave their tokens, and feed that to the LLM. That works surprisingly well. It's a little inelegant, but it's a strong signal that the two kinds of information are complementary and that a single contrastive objective isn't capturing both.

But if I'm designing from scratch, I'd want a single backbone with a multi-objective training recipe. Something like contrastive alignment with text, plus a dense self-supervised objective, maybe masked reconstruction or a DINO-style self-distillation on local patches. The point is that the language loss anchors the global semantics, and the dense loss forces the model to keep the local detail around. There's work moving in this direction, and in my experience the key is weighting and scheduling. If you just add the losses naively, the contrastive term tends to dominate and you end up back where you started.

Second, resolution and token count matter a lot, and I think people underinvest here relative to architecture. Fine-grained discrimination fundamentally needs more pixels. The old default of 224 by 224 with a handful of hundred tokens is just not enough to read a chart or distinguish two sparrow species. So I'd design the encoder to natively handle variable and high resolution, with some kind of adaptive tokenization, so you're not paying for a thousand tokens on a blank image but you can spend them when the image demands it. The LLM side can handle long contexts now, so the bottleneck has shifted to whether the encoder is producing tokens that carry the information in the first place.

Third, and this is maybe the more opinionated part, I'd train the encoder jointly with the LLM for longer than people currently do. There's this habit of freezing the vision encoder during multimodal training, partly because it's cheap and partly out of fear that you'll destroy the pretrained features. But if you freeze it, the encoder never learns what the language model actually needs. I think unfreezing, with a careful learning rate and maybe some regularization toward the original weights, lets the encoder learn to surface fine-grained information in a form that's useful for language reasoning. That's a different thing from being language-aligned in the CLIP sense. It's being aligned to the downstream reasoning process.

And then a last thought. We should probably be more skeptical of how we evaluate this. A lot of the benchmarks people use to say "this encoder is good" are either captioning-ish tasks that reward the CLIP-style global semantics, or they're ImageNet-style classification that rewards something else. Neither really tests whether the model can do fine-grained visual reasoning in a language context. So part of designing the encoder well is just being honest about what you're measuring. If your benchmark can be solved by a blurry global embedding, you'll keep building blurry global encoders.

So in short, multi-objective training, high and adaptive resolution, don't freeze the encoder, and measure the right thing. None of those are individually revolutionary, but I think the combination is where you get an encoder that genuinely does both.

r001.rationale: The response proposes combining text contrastive alignment with a dense self-supervised objective to preserve local visual detail, and also describes combining complementary encoders.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest temporal modeling or world models for the vision component.

astra-6.text:
I would start by recognizing that language alignment and fine-grained visual discrimination are related, but they’re not exactly the same objective. A caption might tell you that there’s a dog in an image, but it usually won’t describe the precise texture of its fur or the position of each paw. So if you train only to align images with text, there’s little incentive to preserve all those details.

My approach would be to combine a language-alignment objective with a visual objective that encourages richer spatial representations—something like self-supervised learning or reconstruction. You want the encoder to learn what matters for language, while retaining information that language supervision doesn’t explicitly capture.

Then the interface to the language model matters a lot. If you compress the image into too few tokens, you can lose fine-grained information even if the encoder originally captured it. I would preserve spatial tokens and potentially use multiple resolutions, with a global view for context and higher-resolution features for small objects or text. You could have separate projection heads for the two objectives, so they don’t have to impose exactly the same structure on the representation.

And I would evaluate both capabilities separately. Better image–text retrieval doesn’t necessarily mean better spatial reasoning or fine-grained recognition. The key question is whether the representation retains the details and whether the language model can actually use them.

r001.rationale: It proposes combining a language-alignment objective with a visual objective that preserves richer spatial and fine-grained information.

r002.rationale: It does not propose temporal modeling or world models for the vision component.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start by separating two things we often ask the vision encoder to do. One is to produce features that align well with language—recognizing the objects and concepts we can describe. The other is to preserve the visual details that language may never explicitly mention: the exact position of an object, a small difference in texture, or the relationship between two nearby regions. Those objectives overlap, but they’re not identical.

So I would consider combining a language-alignment objective with a visual learning objective that preserves local information, such as self-supervised learning over image patches. You could use a shared encoder with different heads, or combine complementary encoders. I’d start with the shared encoder because it’s simpler, and then measure whether the objectives actually interfere.

The interface to the language model also matters. If you compress the entire image into a few tokens too early, you can lose information even with a very good encoder. I would retain spatial features and give the model a way to access higher-resolution regions when the task requires them.

And I’d evaluate these capabilities separately. Good image-text retrieval doesn’t establish that a model can distinguish two very similar objects or read a small detail. The question is whether improving alignment also preserves the information needed for those finer judgments.

r001.rationale: It proposes combining language alignment with a visual learning objective that preserves local information, such as self-supervised learning over image patches.

r002.rationale: It does not propose temporal modeling or world models for the vision component.
